title: Ropes & Gray encourages junior lawyers to spend 20% of billable time on AI (Legal Cheek article + anonymous comment thread)
pub: Legal Cheek (news item with practitioner comment thread beneath)
author: Legal Cheek staff; anonymous Legal Cheek commenters

dom.t: Task substitution: Complementarity can still reshape staffing

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source accepts the need for AI fluency, training and organisational support, and adds concrete examples of firms and legal educators integrating AI into junior development. Its associate scepticism also reinforces the cluster’s warning that effective adoption depends on informed leadership rather than indiscriminate tool promotion.
qs: It seems to be driven by partners who have very little concept of what AI can and cannot do, and who see it as some sort of “magic” tool.

st.t: Task substitution: Complementarity can still reshape staffing
st.an: The source supports task-sensitive complementarity rather than wholesale substitution: reported initiatives invest substantially in junior lawyers’ AI fluency while retaining deep legal reasoning, and anonymous accounts reinforce that usefulness varies by task and that hallucinations constrain reliable adoption. It provides institutional and experiential examples, but no evidence establishing staffing or employment outcomes.
qs: Its ability to research is notoriously poor, and even in the summarization of notes etc I’ve seen it hallucinate.

kp.k: Ropes & Gray allocates junior billable time to AI
kp.d: The November 19, 2025 article reports an initiative encouraging first-year associates to devote around 20% of billable time to AI experimentation and training. Against a reportedly 1,900-hour annual target, the article describes roughly 400 hours for training, simulations and workflow testing. A US pilot is underway, with subsequent expansion planned across 16 offices, including London; the report does not establish completed global implementation or training outcomes.
qs: The Boston-founded firm is rolling out a new global initiative encouraging first-year associates to commit around 20% of their billable time to experimenting and training with AI tools.
With new associates reportedly set a billable target of 1,900 hours a year, juniors would spend roughly 400 of those on AI training, simulations and workflow testing.
A pilot scheme is already underway in the firm’s US offices, with plans to later roll out the initiative across its 16 offices worldwide, including London.

kp.k: Hebbia partnership targets document review and transactional analysis
kp.d: The article links the initiative to Ropes & Gray’s expanded partnership with legal-AI provider Hebbia, announced in August. It describes the platform as designed to improve complex document review and data analysis in high-stakes transactions, including greater speed and precision than many other LLMs, but supplies no comparative measurements or realised results.
qs: This comes after the firm announced an expanded partnership in August with legal AI provider Hebbia, whose platform is designed to optimise complex document review and data analysis in high-stakes transactions with greater speed and precision than many other LLMs.

kp.k: Other firms support innovation and AI-fluent junior development
kp.d: The article reports Reed Smith’s credit for innovation-related projects and Kennedys’ work with Spellbrook to help juniors adapt to changing entry-level work. Following the Kennedys discussion, it quotes senior partner John Bruce framing training as a responsibility to prevent juniors being left behind and to combine deep legal reasoning with AI fluency. These are reported initiatives and a stated developmental objective, rather than evidence of achieved competence.
qs: has also offered credit for
innovation-related projects
is working with generative AI platform Spellbrook to help juniors adapt to the shifting nature of entry-level legal work.

As AI accelerates change across the legal sector, we have a responsibility to ensure junior lawyers aren’t left behind. This programme is about creating AI-fluent lawyers: professionals who can combine deep legal reasoning with the ability to work seamlessly alongside AI tools.

kp.k: Legal education institutions embed Harvey tools and teaching materials
kp.d: The article reports that BPP, ULaw, Oxford and King’s College London struck a deal with Harvey to embed generative AI tools and teaching materials in law courses, research centres and professional training. It references reporting from the preceding day, without presenting implementation or educational outcome evidence.
qs: BPP, ULaw, Oxford and King’s College London have struck a deal with US legal-AI firm Harvey
embedding its generative AI tools and teaching materials into their law courses, research centres and professional training.

kp.k: Associate questions partner-led adoption and practical task reliability
kp.d: An anonymous commenter, self-described as an associate at a US firm in the City, reports on November 19, 2025 that their firm heavily pushes AI. They perceive partners as misunderstanding its capabilities and describe limited usefulness in their own work, poor research and hallucinations in note summarisation. They acknowledge basic email drafting but question its added value. These are individual experiences and perceptions, not measured error rates or representative findings.
qs: It seems to be driven by partners who have very little concept of what AI can and cannot do, and who see it as some sort of “magic” tool.
But I have found that, for much of my work, AI is quite unhelpful.
Its ability to research is notoriously poor, and even in the summarization of notes etc I’ve seen it hallucinate.
It can draft a basic email response. But then so can I…

kp.k: Applicant finds unexplained AI recruitment messaging off-putting
kp.d: A November 20, 2025 anonymous commenter identifying as a law-firm applicant with a STEM background, including computer science and building AI apps, objects to AI-centred strategy and careers presentations lacking substantive explanations. They also report never finding an AI tool that answers a complex legal query entirely accurately. This supplies one applicant’s reaction and experience, not evidence about recruitment effects generally or benchmarked accuracy.
qs: I am a student applying to law firms currently and find it very off-putting when AI takes centre stage of firm strategy/marketing, or when it is thrown into careers presentations as something wonderful and transformative, with no substantive explanations as to how/why it is such.
Very rare that I find an AI tool can answer a complex legal query entirely accurately. Very rare as in never, in fact.

kp.k: Commenters favour appropriate use over indiscriminate AI investment
kp.d: Two further anonymous comments dated November 20, 2025 acknowledge a place for AI while stressing appropriate use. One uses a tool-selection analogy; the other criticises decision-makers’ understanding and asserts that the vast majority of companies investing heavily in AI have not seen worthwhile returns. The return-on-investment assertion is unsupported within the thread and is the commenter’s claim, not a reported study finding.
qs: It’s a good tool when used appropriately. You wouldn’t hammer a nail with a saw.
It absolutely has its place, but I have no time for people pushing business decisions who don’t appear to have even taken a moment to consider what that place might be.
Particularly when the vast majority of companies investing heavily in AI have yet to see any worthwhile ROI.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The article reports institutional investment in junior lawyers’ AI training, while anonymous commenters question the usefulness, reliability and strategic rationale of adoption.
pts.d: Legal Cheek reports that Ropes & Gray is encouraging first-year associates to allocate around 20% of their billable time to AI experimentation and training, with a US pilot and a planned worldwide rollout. It describes Hebbia’s platform as designed to improve the speed and precision of complex document review and data analysis; this is a statement of intended capability, not a demonstrated outcome. The article also reports innovation credit at Reed Smith, Kennedys’ work with Spellbrook to help juniors adapt, and the embedding of Harvey tools and teaching materials in legal education. Senior partner John Bruce, quoted in the article, frames the programme as a way to produce lawyers who combine legal reasoning with AI fluency, rather than replacing lawyers. Anonymous commenter 1 reports limited usefulness for much of their own work, poor research performance and hallucinations in summarisation, while acknowledging basic email drafting capability. Anonymous commenter 2 reports never obtaining an entirely accurate answer to a complex legal query and says AI-centred firm marketing is off-putting. Commenter 3 endorses appropriate, task-specific use. Commenter 4 acknowledges a place for AI but questions decision-makers’ understanding and claims that most companies investing heavily have not seen worthwhile returns.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The article offers reported initiatives, workload figures and a senior partner’s rationale; the comments offer personal experience or unsupported general assertions rather than systematic performance evidence.
pts.d: Legal Cheek supplies the reported 1,900-hour annual target, an approximate 400-hour training allocation, the existing US pilot and the August expansion of the Hebbia partnership as evidence of organisational adoption. These facts concern investment and programme design, not measured productivity, accuracy or training outcomes. No comparative benchmark is supplied for Hebbia’s stated speed and precision. Bruce’s statement is a leadership explanation of programme aims. Commenter 1’s evidence is their self-described experience as an associate at a US firm in the City, including observed hallucinations. Commenter 2 invokes a STEM and computer-science background, experience building AI apps and personal experience with complex legal queries. Neither identifies tested tools, tasks, sample sizes or error rates. Commenters 3 and 4 provide no supporting study or data for their general claims, including commenter 4’s cross-company ROI assertion.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The US pilot is reported as underway in November 2025, with worldwide expansion planned but undated; the comments describe contemporaneous experience and qualify usefulness by task.
pts.d: The article was published on 19 November 2025. Its US pilot is current at publication, while rollout across 16 offices, including London, is a future plan without a completion date. The training allocation is encouraged and approximate, not described as a compulsory quota. The Hebbia partnership expansion is dated to August in the article’s 2025 context. The comments are dated 19–20 November 2025; their August 2026 capture date is not the date of the claims. Bruce’s account of accelerating change has no quantified forecast horizon. Commenter 1 limits the strongest usefulness criticism to much of their own work and acknowledges some capabilities. Commenter 2’s accuracy claim concerns complex legal queries. Commenter 3 makes appropriate use a condition of usefulness. Commenter 4’s ROI assertion concerns returns realised so far, without a defined observation period.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The stated effects concern first-year associates’ training and workflows, firm adoption decisions, legal education and applicant perceptions.
pts.d: Ropes & Gray’s first-year associates are the direct targets of the proposed training allocation, initially in US offices and subsequently worldwide, including London. The firm is described as employing more than 1,500 lawyers across three regions, but the initiative specifically targets first-year associates rather than all lawyers. Lawyers working on complex document review, data analysis and high-stakes transactions are the intended users of the Hebbia capabilities described. Bruce presents junior lawyers as needing support to avoid being left behind. Commenter 1 describes pressure on practising associates from partners perceived as misunderstanding AI. Commenter 2 illustrates a possible recruitment effect: AI-centred strategy and marketing deter this particular applicant, not necessarily applicants generally. The Harvey arrangements affect law courses, research centres and professional training at BPP, ULaw, Oxford and King’s College London. The document does not provide a concrete prediction of job losses, client fee reductions or improved public access to justice.
